headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Puerperal Sepsis
headings.content: Puerperal sepsis is a serious infection of the genital tract that occurs anytime between the rupture of membranes or labor and the 42nd day postpartum. Historically known as childbed fever, it remains a major cause of maternal mortality and morbidity worldwide, particularly in low-resource settings. Clinically, it is defined by the presence of a fever alongside pelvic pain, abnormal vaginal discharge, or delayed uterine involution. Recognizing this condition early is vital because postpartum infections can escalate rapidly from a localized wound infection into overwhelming systemic illness and septic shock.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Common Causative Organisms
headings.content:
Following delivery, the placental site leaves a large, raw, vascular wound inside the uterus that is highly vulnerable to bacterial invasion. Bacteria ascend from the lower genital tract or are introduced during examinations and delivery procedures. 

- **Group A Streptococcus (GAS)**: Highly virulent organism responsible for rapid, severe, and toxic postpartum infections.
- **Staphylococcus aureus**: Commonly found on the skin; frequently implicated in wound infections and mastitis.
- **Escherichia coli**: Enteric bacteria from the bowel that easily contaminate the perineum and ascend into the urinary or genital tract.
- **Anaerobes**: Organisms such as *Bacteroides* species thrive in necrotic tissue and contribute heavily to pelvic abscesses.

headings.title: Risk Factors and Predisposing Conditions
headings.content: Certain obstetric and environmental factors increase a woman's susceptibility to developing puerperal sepsis. Prolonged rupture of membranes allows bacteria in the vagina an open pathway to ascend into the uterine cavity. Multiple vaginal examinations during prolonged labor likewise introduce external pathogens. Cesarean delivery, especially when performed as an emergency procedure after labor has already commenced, carries a much higher infection risk than a normal vaginal delivery. Other contributing factors include anemia, retained placental fragments, obesity, and low socioeconomic status leading to poor hygiene and delayed care.

headings.title: Clinical Presentation and Assessment Findings
headings.content:
The clinical picture of puerperal sepsis usually begins with a postpartum fever, often exceeding 38 degrees Celsius on any two of the first ten days following delivery, excluding the first 24 hours. 

| Assessment Area | Common Clinical Signs |
| --- | --- |
| Vital Signs | Tachycardia, tachypnea, low or unstable blood pressure |
| Uterus | Subinvolution, severe lower abdominal tenderness |
| Lochia | Foul-smelling, purulent, or unusually profuse vaginal discharge |
| General State | Chills, malaise, pelvic pain, confusion in severe cases |

headings.title: Diagnostic Evaluation and Investigations
headings.content: Confirming puerperal sepsis requires a combination of clinical assessment and laboratory investigations. Blood cultures should be drawn before starting antibiotics to isolate the specific causative organism. A complete blood count typically reveals leukocytosis with a shift to the left, indicating active infection. High vaginal swabs or endocervical cultures help identify local pathogens. Urinalysis and urine culture rule out a concurrent urinary tract infection. Pelvic ultrasound is especially useful when retained products of conception or a pelvic abscess is suspected.

headings.title: Medical and Antimicrobial Management
headings.content: Prompt initiation of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics is the cornerstone of treating puerperal sepsis. Therapy is typically started empirically to cover a wide range of gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms before culture results return. Once sensitivities are available, the antibiotic regimen is tailored accordingly. If retained placental tissue is identified on ultrasound, surgical evacuation via curettage or gentle exploration is necessary to remove the source of infection. Supportive fluid resuscitation and vasopressors may be required if the patient progresses toward septic shock.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Supportive Management
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing care focuses on monitoring vital signs closely to detect early signs of clinical deterioration. Nurses administer prescribed intravenous antibiotics precisely on schedule to maintain therapeutic blood levels. Accurate fluid balance monitoring, including strict measurement of urine output via catheterization if necessary, helps evaluate kidney perfusion and cardiovascular status. Providing pain relief, encouraging comfortable positioning, and offering emotional support to the mother are essential aspects of holistic recovery. Nurses must also practice rigorous hand hygiene and aseptic technique during all wound dressings and perineal care.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Prevention Strategies
headings.content: When puerperal sepsis is inadequately managed, it can lead to severe complications including peritonitis, pelvic abscess formation, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and septic shock. Prevention relies heavily on antenatal care that treats maternal anemia, minimizing unnecessary vaginal examinations during labor, maintaining sterile operating conditions during cesarean sections, and administering prophylactic antibiotics when indicated. Educating mothers on recognizing early signs of infection before discharge ensures prompt return to the hospital if symptoms develop.
